title: Ajahn Funn: The Buddha taught us to be steadfast so that we may end demerit and kamma, end all misfortunes. The mind is samādhi, the…
content:
If the Mind Does Not Produce Bhava and Jāti, Then There Is No Birth

The Buddha taught us to be steadfast so that we may end demerit and kamma, end all misfortunes. The mind is samādhi, the mind is steadfast. When the mind is peaceful, all things are peaceful. If this mind does not go to produce bhava and jāti, who will go to produce them? When the mind does not produce them, then birth does not exist. Where would aging come from? When aging does not exist, where would sickness and disease come from? When sickness and disease do not exist, where would death come from? When death does not exist, where would birth come from? It is like this. This is how we wander in saṃsāra, dying and being reborn, being reborn and dying, dying and being reborn, for countless aeons and eons, for infinite time. If we look steadily at the mind, we see that it is we ourselves who produce bhava and jāti. If we stop, then it is the deathless, it is something permanent and true, not changeable. Not going to produce bhava and jāti. When there is no jāti (birth), then there is no jarā (aging). When there is no jarā, then there is no byādhi (sickness). When there is no byādhi, then there is no maraṇa (death). This is how it is.

title: Ajahn Funn: In the past, when they listened, they drew the teaching inwards to their own minds and hearts. Merit arose right then. The mind…
content:
Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho Are Our Refuge Within the Heart

In the past, when they listened, they drew the teaching inwards to their own minds and hearts. Merit arose right then. The mind became cool and refreshed, light and at ease. That is merit itself. Do we have it in our minds? Are we happy and at ease? Right now, as we are sitting here, look and see. Recollect: Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho. Recollect.

Where is Buddho? Where is Dhammo? Where is Saṅgho? This is our refuge and recollection, what we pay homage to, bow to, venerate. If we have no Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho, then we have no refuge. Having Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho is our refuge, our recollection, what we bow to and venerate. Draw it inwards. Where is Buddho? Is it not in our heart? Contemplate Buddho. Right now, what do you know? Do you know happiness or suffering? Do you know good or evil? Or do you know just neutral? Look at Buddho. Where is your mind abiding? Is it in the wind and air, or somewhere else? Is it with your children and grandchildren, with your home and possessions, or with your rice, belongings, money, and gold? Draw it inwards to yourself. One who knows the religion must draw it inwards, must know the root of the religion.

title: Ajahn Funn: If I keep explaining like this, there’s no end. To sum up, it all comes down to this body and mind. Focus, contemplate:…
content:
Transcending Suffering Means the Mind Does Not Suffer

If I keep explaining like this, there’s no end. To sum up, it all comes down to this body and mind. Focus, contemplate: good and evil, both external and internal, have been explained so that you know. Now, opanayiko – is it real or not? Let us all focus: where is it stuck? Where is it caught? Where is it not yet resolved? Focus right there. Do not send it forward, backward, left, right, above, below. Set it right at the middle, at that which knows. This is it. Whatever it is like, we keep correcting it there, keep purifying it there. That is what is meant by looking – not looking at anything else. Look at our own mind, look at our own becoming, look at our own refuge. Look so that you know. Whether the seat is good or not, we must know right here. Sanditthiko – the practitioner knows for themselves, sees for themselves. If we don’t know, others can tell us but we won’t know. This is how the practice is. From now on, whatever sound you hear, remind yourself: that thing is harmless, we need not be troubled. Make your mind… I will not explain further. Let us become calm. Each one calm down. Let go, make yourself comfortable. We want happiness and ease, so that it becomes our merit and our spiritual potential, so that we transcend suffering. We all want to transcend suffering – look: transcending suffering means our mind is not suffering. When our mind does not suffer, then we have transcended suffering. It is not about transcending in the sky or air. Look: if it is still suffering, it has not transcended suffering.

title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore, we must first examine our own heart. Otherwise we won’t know how to correct it. Old kamma is not yet exhausted, and…
content:
Suppressing Kamma: Making the Mind Calm, Still, and Neutral

Therefore, we must first examine our own heart. Otherwise we won’t know how to correct it. Old kamma is not yet exhausted, and new kamma keeps adding on. When we suppress kamma, we cause our mind to become calm, still, and neutral – not sending it forward, not to the left, right, above, or below. Only awareness remains. Investigate: is it good or not? Where is it stuck? Where is it caught? What is lacking or deficient? Then we cleanse and rectify it. This is the practice to attain virtue and Dhamma, to attain the religion. Religion is a tool for ending suffering. Religion exists for the sake of suffering. Now, where does suffering come from? We must listen and observe to see the suffering in our own mind. Suffering – why? Suffering because of delusion. When our mind is not calm, it suffers. When our mind is not good, it suffers.

For this reason, you must know right down to its root. It is like a gardener tending his orchard. He must nurture the tree, fertilize it, water it. If the tree is good, you don’t need to tell or force the branches – it will produce beautiful flowers and fruit. If the tree is good, its fruit will be abundant. This simile is given for you to see. If the tree is not good, it will have no flowers, no fruit. Just so with our mind.

title: Ajahn Funn: We are practitioners of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). What shall we establish as our foundation? Greed, anger, and delusion are the roots of the unwholesome…
content:
Greed, Anger, and Delusion Have a Single Root – The Mind

We are practitioners of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). What shall we establish as our foundation? Greed, anger, and delusion are the roots of the unwholesome (akusala), leading to decline and ruin for oneself. Non-greed, non-anger, and non-delusion are the roots of the wholesome (kusala), leading to prosperity and growth for oneself. Ekamūlā — all things have a single root. Greed, anger, and delusion have this mind as their root. Non-greed, non-anger, and non-delusion also have this very same mind as their root cause. Hence they are called ekamūlā — having a single root cause, namely the mind. If the mind is not greedy, then nothing is greedy. If the mind is not angry, then nothing is angry. If the mind is not deluded, then nothing is deluded. A dead person without breath — that is a person without a mind. You don't see a dead person greedily wanting anything. You don't see a dead person raging with anger at anyone. You don't see a dead person deluded about anything. Only those who still have this mind — they still have deluded love and deluded hate.

title: Ajahn Funn: When you practice meditation until it becomes established and the mind becomes tranquil and still, then there arises within a great gentleness and…
content:
When the Mind Becomes Tranquil: Lighter Than Cotton Wool

When you practice meditation until it becomes established and the mind becomes tranquil and still, then there arises within a great gentleness and tenderness, a coolness of heart and mind, lighter than cotton wool. Our mind is just like the breath; it’s at ease, all pain and suffering disappears. Sitting on a wooden plank feels like not sitting at all. It becomes completely still. It remains observing. It doesn’t take up anything else because it has seen the cause (samuṭṭhāna). Just like a doctor: once he sees the cause, he prescribes the right medicine. At this point, it sees the cause: that such-and-such things lead to making merit and demerit, to kamma. That is, the mind-element (cittadhātu) that doesn’t stop, doesn’t stay still; the ambitious, restless mind-element that runs about, creating demerit, creating kamma, creating realms of existence and births: bhave bhavā sambhavanti — small realms, great realms — it goes about creating them. Even while sitting, it is still creating.

title: Ajahn Funn: The Buddha taught us to do this, for people to believe in the Buddha. He did not establish the teaching in trees, mountains,…
content:
The Buddha Established the Teaching Right Here: Sīla, Samādhi, Paññā

The Buddha taught us to do this, for people to believe in the Buddha. He did not establish the teaching in trees, mountains, hills, caves, jungles, villages, cities, roads, or in halls, monasteries, or Dhamma halls. He established the teaching right here in each of us: that is sīla, samādhi, paññā. This has been explained. Restrain our body, speech, and mind. Our body is the Buddha's teaching; our speech is the Buddha's teaching; our mind is the Buddha's teaching. The Buddha responded to our body, our speech, our mind. He taught us to do good, not to do evil, to leave it empty. You all have studied much. You already know what is wrong and what is right. Do not do what is bad. If we do not do it, then bad things will not come to us. If we do it, then those things necessarily come. We practice samādhi, make the mind steadfast, look at our mind. Where is our mind? The mind is the one that thinks, that remembers, that concocts, that fabricates. Who is it that does merit and demerit, produces bhava and jāti, produces kamma and enmity?

title: Ajahn Funn: Contemplate this so that you see it clearly and manifestly for yourselves. We come to make merit and wholesome deeds. We ask: does…
content:
Merit Is Known by the Heart: After Giving, Does Your Mind Feel Cool and Refreshed?

Contemplate this so that you see it clearly and manifestly for yourselves. We come to make merit and wholesome deeds. We ask: does this giving produce merit? Does that giving produce merit? Ask whom? Ask your own heart. If after doing it, your heart feels cool and refreshed, your mind is happy, your mind is at ease, then merit is right there.

Therefore, for all merits, mind comes first. For evil, too, mind comes first. Our mind is the foundation, the presiding factor. It is accomplished with the heart, not accomplished anywhere far away. Hence you should all contemplate with certainty, see it clearly, have confidence in it. This, in summary, is the essential point of the Buddha's exhortation and teaching: this body and mind are the foundation for the qualities of the Buddha, the qualities of the Dhamma, and the qualities of the Sangha.

When we have heard this, we should apply wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), remember it well, and then go on to practice and train ourselves, so that we have confidence in sīla, confidence in the Dhamma, the teaching of the Supreme Perfectly Enlightened Buddha. From now on, all of you will have only happiness, prosperity, and growth in the Dhamma and discipline of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.

title: Ajahn Funn: Having heard this, then opanayiko – bring it inside and look within. Do people die and then get reborn? Look at ourselves: are…
content:
Washing Away Kamma by Sitting in Samādhi Until the Mind Is Peaceful

Having heard this, then opanayiko – bring it inside and look within. Do people die and then get reborn? Look at ourselves: are we being reborn right now? Are we doing it right now? Is our mind staying still? Come on, bring the opanayika dhamma and look inside. Can our mind stay still? It is producing bhava and jāti – who knows how many bhava? It concocts, it fabricates, it produces there, it ceases here, produces there. It goes on like that. How many bhava has it been? Right now as we sit here, this birth – we cannot prevent it. That is why the Buddha taught us to contemplate buddho.

At the same time, he taught us to contemplate these devadūta, bring them up within our own mind. Suffering, which is this birth, we must stop it. Wash away demerit and kamma, cut off demerit and kamma. We cannot wash it away with a knife or a sword, nor with water. Only by sitting in samādhi until the mind is peaceful. When the mind is peaceful, it is empty, nothing at all. There is only lightness and ease, cool body and cool mind, ending suffering and difficulty, ending trouble and vexation. Only buddho, the joy; buddho, the brightness; buddho, the clarity. All kamma ends, all evil ends. Only buddho, the joy. Therefore, our refuge must depend on this knowledge.

title: Ajahn Funn: What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? When the mind is in the sensual plane, it roams among…
content:
Transcending the Sensual Plane: Contemplating the Body to Generate Disenchantment

What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? When the mind is in the sensual plane, it roams among forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, and mental phenomena (dhammārammaṇa) – that is its object. It is called one who delights in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, contacts, and various mental objects. This is called the mind abiding in the sensual-sphere realm (kāmāvacara bhūmi), in the existence called the sensual realm (kāmabhava).

What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? It lets go of external forms, external sounds, external smells, external tastes, and the many contacts and mental objects. It sees only this individual body of ours. It contemplates this conditioned body of ours, fixed right on itself, not sending the mind elsewhere or far away. It sees only our own conditioned body – its deterioration, its decay, or sees the conditioned body exactly as it is: with hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin. There is nothing else beyond this, nothing superior to this. Whether happiness or suffering, seeing deterioration and decay, or seeing breaking apart, the mind then abandons this form. Nibbidā arises – disenchantment with this form. Because this form has no core, no substance, no essence.
